title: Design exercise: news feed
summary: A classic design exercise: the home feed of a social product with a heavy-tailed follower graph. The reference answer sizes fan-out from stated assumptions, chooses hybrid fan-out (on write for most authors, on read for celebrities), keeps a bounded timeline cache of post ids per user, ranks at read time behind a deadline, and treats fan-out lag as the freshness SLI.

exercise.prompt: Design the home feed of a social product: a user follows other users and sees their recent posts, newest or best first, every time they open the app. Posting must feel instant and the feed must open fast even for people who follow thousands of accounts.

constraints.caption: Constraints and numbers.
rows: Create a post (text, optional media reference); follow and unfollow; read the home feed with paging.
A post appears in followers' feeds within seconds; an unfollow removes the author's future posts from the feed.
50 million registered users, 10 million daily active.
Each user follows 200 accounts on average; a few thousand accounts have more than 1 million followers.
2 million posts per day; each active user opens the feed 10 times a day.
Peak rates are 10 times the daily average.
derive the per-second rates, the fan-out volume and the timeline cache size yourself
Feed open p99 under 200 ms from the service.
A post visible to followers within 5 s at p99.
99.9 percent availability for reads; posting may be less available than reading.
A feed holds the latest 800 post ids per user.
the public Twitter talk describes a bounded in-memory timeline per user
Search, direct messages, ads, media transcoding, the ranking model itself.
ranking is a service with a known latency

clarifying_questions.a: Ranked, but the candidate set is chronological: the last few hundred posts from followed accounts, re-ordered by a ranking service at read time.

clarifying_questions.q: How fresh must the feed be?
clarifying_questions.a: A new post should be visible within 5 s; a few seconds of staleness in the ranked order is fine.
Heavy-tailed: a median user has a few hundred followers; a few thousand accounts have millions.

clarifying_questions.q: Do deletes and unfollows have to be immediate?
clarifying_questions.a: A deleted post must never render; it may stay in cached id lists and be filtered at read time. Unfollow stops future posts; past ones may linger until they age out.

clarifying_questions.q: Is the feed read when the user is offline?
clarifying_questions.a: No; feeds are computed for active users only. A user inactive for 30 days (assumption) has no cached timeline and gets one rebuilt on return.

clarifying_questions.q: Can a reader see a post the author later restricts?
clarifying_questions.a: Visibility is checked at render time against the current setting, never baked into the cache.

blocks.text: Every number below follows from the stated assumptions: 10 million daily active users who each follow 200 accounts and open the feed 10 times a day, 2 million posts a day, and a peak at ten times the daily average. The tables carry the arithmetic; the paragraphs carry the assumptions.

blocks.caption: Rates and daily volumes derived from the assumptions.
rows: 2 million posts times 200 followers; each append is one 16-byte entry (post id plus timestamp) onto a per-user list
400 million divided by 10 million; the unit the cost line is priced in
2 million posts times 1 kB, before media; 730 GB per year in the post store

blocks.text: The fan-out row rests on one piece of graph arithmetic: in a closed graph every follow edge has one follower and one followee, so the mean follower count equals the mean followee count, 200. The row also assumes posts are spread evenly over authors; posts by accounts with millions of followers would raise the post-weighted average, and the celebrity exception below is what keeps them out of the fan-out path. The write amplification of 200 is the price of a cheap read.

blocks.caption: Sizes: the timeline cache and the post store.
rows: an 8-byte post id plus an 8-byte timestamp; with time-ordered ids the timestamp is redundant and the entry could be halved, so 16 bytes is conservative
12.8 kB times 10 million active users: a small cluster of memory nodes
Memory per active user with one replica
two copies of the 12.8 kB timeline
2 GB per day times 2; serves nearly every feed render
2 GB per day times 365, before media

blocks.text: Reading a feed from the cache is one lookup of a few hundred ids plus one batched fetch of post content. A main memory reference costs about 100 ns and a round trip inside the datacenter about 500 microseconds, so the read path sits far inside the 200 ms budget.

Assembling the feed at read time from 200 followed accounts instead means 200 lookups whose slowest reply sets the latency. The Tail at Scale shows that the p99 of such a fan-out is dominated by its worst member, which is why this answer precomputes the timeline for most users and reserves read-time assembly for the few celebrity accounts.

blocks.caption: Cost per daily active user. Both unit prices are assumptions chosen to make the arithmetic concrete.
rows: 25.6 kB per user, the timeline and one replica
Fan-out appends and the workers' compute
40 appends a day, about 1,200 a month
fan-out compute, not the cache, is the larger line; the celebrity threshold is the lever on it

blocks.text: That total per daily active user per month is the number the team is held to. It is set before the design, not read off the bill afterwards, and the table shows which line the design can move.

A post is stored once and its id is pushed, asynchronously, into the timeline cache of every follower: fan-out on write. The feed service reads the user's cached ids, merges in recent posts from the few celebrity accounts the user follows (fan-out on read for those only), asks the ranking service to order the candidates, and renders content from a post cache.

blocks.legend: Boxes are containers; the two frames are the write and read paths; cylinders are stores; double brackets are logs.

blocks.text: The primer's Twitter worked solution describes this shape in text: a fan-out service stores each tweet in the home timeline of every follower in a memory cache, keeps several hundred entries per timeline, rebuilds the timeline of a user inactive for 30 days from the database, and advises against fanning out tweets from highly followed users, merging them at serve time instead.

The public Twitter talk is the first-hand account of the same hybrid: fan-out on write into bounded in-memory timelines, with highly followed accounts handled differently. LinkedIn's FollowFeed chose the opposite default, fan-out on read over a timeline index, after measuring that materialised feeds made the stored data 62 times larger than the pull model; this answer uses that shape only for celebrities.

blocks.legend: The write half of the architecture, the same boxes as the neutral diagram's write path, one AWS service each: the post service and the fan-out workers are ECS on Fargate tasks, the posts store and the social graph are DynamoDB tables, the post events log is an SQS standard queue, and the timeline cache is an ElastiCache for Valkey cluster. CloudFront and the load balancer are the edge the neutral diagram leaves implicit. Each arrow says how the call is made: HTTPS from clients, HTTP inside the VPC, named AWS SDK calls over VPC endpoints, SQS long-poll, cache writes. Sync means the caller waits for the answer; async means the work goes on after the caller has been answered. The VPC frames are one VPC in one Region across three Availability Zones, drawn apart so each frame's title stays readable. DynamoDB and SQS are Regional services outside the VPC, reached through endpoints, while the cache lives inside it. The posts box also stands for the small table of idempotency keys, and the follows box also holds the follower-count items. The flow draws the main path of a post and of its fan-out; the sequence diagrams below also show the media upload to S3, the key item, the follower-count read at post time, the follow calls and the dedupe, which the flow leaves out. The SendMessage is a synchronous call, since the 201 waits for it, even though the arrow is drawn as the hand-off to the queue's asynchronous consumers.

CloudFront, the load balancer and the timeline cache appear in both halves. Every arrow here is synchronous: HTTPS from clients, HTTP inside the VPC, a named SDK call over the gateway endpoint, cache reads; the cache clusters keep one replica per shard in another zone. The flow draws the main path of a read; the sequence diagrams below also show the follows-table reads for a rebuild, the celebrity set, the pending followees, the content fill and the cache fills. Where the flow says MGET, keys that sit in different hash slots cannot share one MGET, so the feed service sends one MGET per hash slot or GETs pipelined per node.

blocks.text: The media upload is sync for the author but outside the post service, which never carries media bytes: the app asks the post service for a presigned URL (POST /media, a local signature) and uploads with it s51, and a failed upload fails before the post is created. The author_id index follows the write within a fraction of a second. Every call from a task to DynamoDB, SQS or S3 goes over a VPC endpoint and never touches the internet. The posts table is on-demand, so the recurring daily peak needs no capacity change; a spike well beyond any earlier peak can still throttle, and the SDK retry in the last branch rides it out.

The app makes an idempotency key for each post. The post service mints the Snowflake post id, writes the key item (author and key, with the post id, eligible for deletion after 24 hours: DynamoDB removes it within a few days, and a read treats an expired item as absent) and then the post, each with a condition, so a retry with the same key finds the key and answers with the same post id, even when the first attempt stopped between the two writes.

Part b: the hand-off to the queue, after the PutItem of part a and before the 201, with the author's follower count read for the celebrity flag, and the 503 this design returns when the queue is unreachable.

blocks.legend: The send at step 12 is a synchronous call and the 201 waits for it; the queue's consumers are the asynchronous part. The follower count read at step 10 gives the celebrity flag. Sources: the interface endpoint s39; the SDK retry s43; the conditional PutItem s44.

blocks.text: The 503 is this design's choice, not an AWS behaviour: the retry it provokes finds the key item, repeats the post PutItem as a no-op and sends again, and a duplicate event is harmless because the feed service drops repeated ids. The follower count is an approximate counter moved by the follow calls (part d); the post service compares it with the threshold and the event carries the flag, so the workers never count followers. A post stored while its event never goes out (the 503 and an app that is not reopened) is found by nothing: the app keeps the key and retries when it reopens, and an alarm watches the 503 rate; no sweep is drawn.
Part c: the fan-out, asynchronous from the author's point of view, starting when a worker receives the event sent at step 12.

blocks.text: The worker never answers anyone: its only signal is the DeleteMessage, so every failure above ends in a redelivery and a redo. The alarm on the dead-letter queue is the one human-facing step.

LPUSH puts the id at the head of the list without looking for it first s50, so a redelivered event appends the same id again. The feed service drops repeated ids when it merges the timeline with the celebrity and backfill ids (read part b), and a repeat holds one of the 800 slots until the trim removes it. The post itself is stored once, by the idempotency key.

The default visibility timeout is 30 seconds s41 and the largest fan-out, a million followers at 5,000 appends a second per task, takes 200 seconds. The worker therefore extends the timeout with ChangeMessageVisibility as a heartbeat while it works through the pages s41, or the queue's timeout is set above the longest fan-out.

Two failure rows are an alarm and a rule, not a branch of a diagram: fan-out lag grows (the workers scale on lag, an alarm watches it) and a viral post by an author under the threshold (batched appends, and the threshold is read at post time).

blocks.legend: Solid arrows are synchronous calls with their replies dashed. Edge is CloudFront in front of the load balancer, as in part a. The count is an atomic counter s48 moved by a second call, so it is approximate; the three cache keys of one user carry the same hash tag and sit in one slot s49. A follow of a celebrity drops the follower's celebrity set instead of adding to it, so no set is ever partial: the next read builds it whole (read part a2). The unfollow moves the count only when the delete returned an item, since an atomic counter is not idempotent s48.

blocks.text: A follow writes the follow item, indexed by followee for the fan-out and, through an index, by follower for the rebuild, and moves the author's follower count with an atomic counter s48. The count is approximate because the two writes are not one transaction, and a follow wave on one celebrity is limited by what one counter item takes, so the call may be throttled and retried. The pending set and the celebrity set of the follower sit in the timeline cache beside the timeline. The follow does not touch the timeline: the next read does (read part a2).

blocks.text: The read path through AWS, part a: getting the timeline ids, with the rebuild on a cache miss.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber

  participant Edge
  participant FS as Feed svc
  participant TL as Timeline cache
  participant DDB as DynamoDB
  App->>Edge: GET /feed, per user
  Note over App,Edge: never cached at the edge
  Edge->>FS: HTTP, a healthy task
  FS->>TL: LRANGE, capped list
  TL-->>FS: post ids
  opt cache miss
    FS->>DDB: Query followees, follows table
    DDB-->>FS: followee ids
    FS->>DDB: Query the author_id index
    DDB-->>FS: recent post ids
    FS->>TL: write the list back
  end
  Note over FS: ids in hand, on to the next part
blocks.legend: Every arrow is synchronous: the reader waits for the whole path, parts a to c. The DynamoDB lane is both tables, the follows table and the posts table with its index. Sources: CloudFront in front of the load balancer s25, s33; health checks and task replacement s31, s32; the capped list and the rebuild s4, s8; the author_id index s30; the gateway endpoint s37.

blocks.text: A cache miss at step 3 is a new user, one back after 30 days, or a shard whose data was lost; the rebuilt first page is served slower. On a feed-service task failure the health check takes it out of service and the client's retry lands on another task. The page starts at the first id smaller than the cursor, which works because the ids are time-ordered; the feed service reads the whole capped list (800 ids) with one LRANGE.
Part a2: the celebrity set and the lazy backfill, which the next reads do for the follow calls of part d.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram autonumber 10 participant FS as Feed svc participant TL as Timeline cache participant DDB as DynamoDB FS->>TL: SMEMBERS the celebrity set
and the pending set TL-->>FS: both sets opt the celebrity set is missing FS->>DDB: Query the followees,
BatchGetItem their counts DDB-->>FS: the counts FS->>TL: SADD the marker and the ones at
800,000 or more, EXPIRE 7 days end opt followees are pending FS->>DDB: Query the author_id index,
last 48 hours, per followee DDB-->>FS: their recent post ids FS->>TL: write the list back merged,
SREM the pending ones end Note over FS: celebrity ids and list ready,
on to part b
blocks.legend: Every arrow is synchronous. The three keys of one user carry the same hash tag, so the two SMEMBERS calls could travel with the LRANGE of part a in one pipeline s49, and are drawn after the rebuild. The set is written whole in one MULTI with its EXPIRE and a marker member that is no author's id: a set with no member is no key s8, so without the marker an empty answer could not be told from a missing set. The DynamoDB lane is the follows table with its follower index and the follower counts, and the posts table with its author_id index.

blocks.text: The celebrity set, the neutral list of the celebrities a user follows, is cached per user beside the timeline and built whole when it is missing: the followees' follower counts are read once, and the set holds the followees at 800,000 followers or more, below the 1 million at which fan-out stops, plus a marker member that is no author's id, written with its seven-day TTL in one transaction. A set with no member is no key s8, so the marker is what tells a built set that is empty of celebrities from a missing one; without it the rebuild would run on every open. A follow of a celebrity drops the set and the next read builds it again with the new followee, so no set is ever partial. A follower whose set predates an author's crossing still gets the posts, because the author was in the band and so was fanned out and merged, the repeat dropped; only an author who goes from under 800,000 to over 1 million followers within one TTL waits for the sets to expire, up to seven days.

The pending set holds the followees followed since the last read: the read that finds one merges that followee's last 48 hours of posts into the timeline and clears the mark, so a wave of follows costs one read each and no write at follow time. A lost cache node loses both sets with the timeline, and the rebuild reads the current follows, so nothing stays pending.
Part b: merging the celebrity posts and ranking, with the throttle and timeout fallbacks.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram autonumber 18 participant FS as Feed svc participant DDB as DynamoDB posts participant RK as Ranking Note over FS: timeline ids from part a FS->>DDB: Query the
author_id index Note over FS,DDB: the celebrity set of part a2 DDB-->>FS: celebrity post ids,
merged by time FS->>FS: drop repeated post ids opt the celebrity Query is throttled FS->>DDB: SDK retry with backoff Note over FS,DDB: still failing: served without them, counted end FS->>RK: candidates with features Note over FS,RK: by Service Connect name, 50 ms client deadline RK-->>FS: ranked ids opt ranking timeout or error Note over FS,RK: chronological order, fallback counted end Note over FS: ranked ids, on to part c
blocks.legend: Sources: the author_id index s30; the SDK retry s43; Service Connect round-robin with outlier detection s36. The repeated ids come from a redelivered event, and the same step covers the ids merged in from part a2 s50.

blocks.text: The candidates go to the ranking service with the user id. The ranking service looks the features up itself, in a feature store this exercise does not design and does not price.
Part c: hydrating the content and returning the page.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram autonumber 24 participant App as Reader's app participant Edge participant FS as Feed svc participant PC as Content cache participant DDB as DynamoDB posts Note over FS: ranked ids from part b FS->>PC: GET the entries,
pipelined per node PC-->>FS: content, with misses opt content misses FS->>DDB: BatchGetItem, gateway endpoint DDB-->>FS: items, written back to the cache end FS->>FS: drop deleted entries FS-->>Edge: page with a cursor Edge-->>App: page Note over App,Edge: media URLs on CloudFront
blocks.legend: Sources: the content cache and DAX as its alternative s26; the gateway endpoint s37; media on CloudFront s25. Keys of different slots cannot share one MGET, so the content reads go out as GETs pipelined per node, or one MGET per hash slot s49.

blocks.text: Deleted and visibility flags are read at render time from the content, never from the timeline list, and the feed service drops those entries from the page. Nothing in the read path writes to DynamoDB; the writes are to the caches: the rebuild and the merge of a pending followee, the celebrity set, and the content fill.

blocks.caption: The posts store and the social graph: DynamoDB, Aurora or RDS, Keyspaces, Neptune.

rows.pick_when: every hot-path access is a key lookup or a single-partition query, the write rate is small or spiky, and nobody wants to plan capacity
rows.avoid_when: the hot path needs joins, ad hoc queries or transactions that span several entities
rows.example: For this design: chosen for both tables. A post is read by post id, the celebrity merge is one query on the author_id index, and follows are adjacency lists keyed by followee with a reverse index; on-demand takes the recurring peak without a capacity change.

rows.option: Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL or Amazon RDS
rows.pick_when: the product needs joins, ad hoc reporting queries or multi-row transactions, or the team's relational skills and tooling are the asset to keep
rows.avoid_when: the access pattern is a handful of key lookups whose rate would keep two always-on instances busy for nothing
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. Nothing on the hot path joins, and two always-on instances would cost about three times the DynamoDB bill after a year of posts for a shape the key-value store already serves.

rows.pick_when: the team already writes CQL and runs Cassandra, or needs wide rows with clustering columns and a path off a self-managed ring
rows.avoid_when: there is no Cassandra estate to move and DynamoDB's partition-key model already fits
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. It offers the same partition-key model without the Cassandra heritage to justify it; picking it would be habit, not requirement.

rows.pick_when: the product needs multi-hop traversals such as friends of friends, paths or recommendations over the graph
rows.avoid_when: the graph is only read as adjacency lists (who follows whom, one hop each way)
rows.example: For this design: not chosen for the social graph. Fan-out needs one hop, the followers of one author, which is one partition in the follows table; a graph database would be paid for traversals the feed never makes.

blocks.caption: The post events: SQS, SNS, EventBridge, or a stream (Kinesis Data Streams, Amazon MSK).

rows.pick_when: one consumer group, at-least-once delivery is fine because the work is idempotent, no ordering across producers is needed, and consumers pull and scale on queue depth
rows.avoid_when: several independent consumers need every event, or consumers must replay history
rows.example: For this design: chosen. The fan-out workers are the only consumer, a redelivery appends the id again and the feed service drops the repeat, and a lost timeline is rebuilt from the posts table rather than by replaying events; ordering per author is not needed because the feed is ranked at read time.

rows.option: Amazon SNS topic in front of one SQS queue per consumer
rows.pick_when: a second consumer appears (search indexing, notifications) and each needs its own queue, retry and dead-letter queue; subscription filters route by message attributes
rows.avoid_when: there is one consumer, so the topic is an extra hop and an extra bill for nothing
rows.example: For this design: not yet. The day search indexing or notifications subscribe to post events, a topic goes in front of the fan-out queue and the post service's SendMessage becomes a Publish; nothing else changes.

rows.pick_when: events of many shapes are routed by rules to many targets, across accounts or to SaaS endpoints, and the routing logic matters more than throughput
rows.avoid_when: one high-volume stream of identical events goes to one worker pool
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. Post events have one shape and one consumer; rule-based routing buys nothing here.

rows.option: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams or Amazon MSK
rows.pick_when: consumers need per-key ordering, replay of retained history, or many independent readers of the same stream at high throughput
rows.avoid_when: the volume is small, nobody replays, and the shard or broker management would be paid for nothing
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. About 2 GB of post events a day with one consumer and no replay need; per-author ordering is not required because the timeline is ranked at read time.

blocks.caption: The post service, the feed service, the fan-out workers and ranking: Lambda, ECS on Fargate or EKS.

rows.option: AWS Lambda, with API Gateway in front where it serves an API
rows.pick_when: traffic is spiky or low, each request is short and stateless, and paying per request beats paying for idle tasks; API Gateway usage plans add per-client throttling and keys
rows.avoid_when: the load is steady and high, the handler must hold connections or batch across events, or per-request billing at billions of calls dwarfs the compute
rows.example: For this design: only for event-shaped side jobs such as thumbnails. The feed service holds persistent connections to the cache at a steady rate, where per-request billing costs about four times the Fargate tasks; the workers batch appends per cache node across many posts, which one invocation per event cannot do.

rows.pick_when: steady, container-shaped services that hold connections, batch work or run longer than a request, and the team wants no cluster to patch
rows.avoid_when: the load is bursty and mostly idle, or the platform team already runs Kubernetes for everything else
rows.example: For this design: chosen for all four services, on Arm (Graviton) tasks across three Availability Zones, scaled on request rate for the post, feed and ranking services and on queue depth and fan-out lag for the workers.

rows.pick_when: the organisation already runs Kubernetes, needs its ecosystem (operators, a service mesh, custom schedulers) or portability across clouds
rows.avoid_when: four stateless services and no Kubernetes estate; the cluster fee, the upgrade cadence and the SRE time buy nothing
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. Nothing here needs the Kubernetes API, and a cluster brings three major releases a year to track for the same four containers.

blocks.caption: The timeline cache and the post content cache: ElastiCache nodes, ElastiCache Serverless, DAX or MemoryDB.

rows.option: Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey, node-based cluster
rows.pick_when: the working set is known and held all month, so memory by the node-hour is cheaper than memory by the GB-hour, and the team can size shards and keep one replica per shard
rows.avoid_when: the working set is small or swings widely, so sized nodes sit idle
rows.example: For this design: chosen for both caches. The timeline working set is a steady 128 GB held all month, and the capped lists need LPUSH, LTRIM and LRANGE, which Valkey gives natively; a replica per shard in another zone covers a node loss.

rows.pick_when: the working set is unpredictable or small and nobody wants to size shards; it scales on its own and bills data stored per GB-hour plus requests in ECPUs
rows.avoid_when: a large working set held all month, because the storage charge then costs more than the equivalent nodes
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. The appends themselves would be cheap in ECPUs, but the timelines stored all month would cost about twice the node cluster.

rows.pick_when: the cache is a read-through in front of a DynamoDB table, reads are plain item lookups, and the team wants one fewer cache to run
rows.avoid_when: the cached structure is not a table item, such as a capped list per user
rows.example: For this design: a candidate for the post content cache only, since a content read is an item lookup on the posts table; the timeline cache cannot be DAX because a timeline is a list, not an item.

rows.pick_when: the in-memory data must survive a node loss without a rebuild, because it is the system of record
rows.avoid_when: the data is a cache that can be rebuilt from a store at an acceptable cost
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. A lost timeline is rebuilt from the posts table within the 48-hour bound, so paying for durable in-memory storage would pay for the data twice.

Everything else together is about 23 percent of the bill, so the levers are the cache's usable memory per node and the celebrity threshold, which moves work between fan-out and read time.

rows: post_id, author_id, created_at, text, media_ref, visibility, deleted
post_id, a time-ordered 64-bit id in the Snowflake layout (41 bits of milliseconds, 10 bits of worker id, 12 bits of sequence); sharded by post_id
visibility and deleted are read at render time, never baked into a cache; the server mints the id, and the client's idempotency key maps to it for retries
indexed both ways: by followee_id (followers of X, for fan-out) and by follower_id (followees of Y, for the celebrity merge)

user_id, then the followee ids not yet merged

user_id, then a list of (post_id, created_at)
partitioned by user_id across memory nodes

user_id, then the list of celebrity ids the user follows

small, cached per user, read on every feed open for the merge; built whole from the followees' follower counts (authors from 800,000 followers) with a marker member and a 7-day TTL, dropped by a follow of a celebrity so the next read builds it again, and cleaned by an unfollow

blocks.caption: The API.
rows: a presigned URL for one upload: the bytes go to the object store, never through the post service
returns once the post is durable; the client makes the key, the server mints the post_id, and a retry with the same key returns the same post_id; fan-out is asynchronous
backfill of the followee's recent posts is lazy: the follow marks the followee pending, and the follower's next read merges the last 48 hours; the follow also moves the followee's follower count
stops future posts and moves the count down; past ones age out of the timeline
cursor: the smallest post id on the previous page
time-ordered ids make paging stable while new posts arrive at the top

blocks.text: The cursor is the smallest post id on the page. Because ids are time-ordered, a page boundary is also a time boundary, so new posts arriving at the top never shift the pages below it, and a client can resume from a cursor after any delay.

reference_answer.title: The core flow, step by step

blocks.text: Posting and reading, in the order a request sees them.
Part a: the author posts and is answered before any fan-out; the step numbers run on across the five parts.

sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant A as Author
  participant PS as Post service
  participant PDB as Posts store
  A->>PS: post
  PS->>PDB: write the post
  PDB-->>PS: durable
  Note over PS: hand-off, part b
  PS-->>A: accepted, before any fan-out
  Note over A,PS: feels instant at any follower count
blocks.legend: Solid arrows are synchronous calls with their replies dashed; the author is answered at step 4, before any fan-out.

blocks.text: Part b: the hand-off to the queue and the fan-out of the post id into the followers' timelines.

sequenceDiagram
  autonumber 5

blocks.legend: The open arrows are the hand-offs through the queue; nothing here is on the author's path. The celebrity branch is decided at post time: the post service compares the author's follower count with the threshold and the event carries the flag, which is what the diagram's mark is. A redelivered event appends the same id again, and the feed service drops repeated ids when it merges.

blocks.legend: The read path begins; every arrow from here to the page is synchronous.

blocks.text: Part d: the celebrity posts are merged in and the candidates ranked, with the chronological fallback.

sequenceDiagram autonumber 16 participant FS as Feed service participant PDB as Posts store participant RK as Ranking Note over FS: timeline ids from part c FS->>PDB: recent posts of
followed celebrities PDB-->>FS: merged by time FS->>RK: candidate ids with features Note over FS,RK: deadline 50 ms (assumption) RK-->>FS: ranked opt timeout Note over FS,RK: chronological order, marked unranked end Note over FS: ranked ids, on to part e
blocks.legend: The merge is a read of the posts store for the few celebrities the user follows; the ranker is on the critical path only up to its deadline.

blocks.text: The celebrities a user follows are cached per user, so step 16 is a handful of lookups.
Part e: the content of the top entries is fetched and the page returned.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram autonumber 20 participant R as Reader participant FS as Feed service participant PC as Post cache Note over FS: ranked ids from part d FS->>PC: content of
the top entries PC-->>FS: content, deleted or restricted dropped FS-->>R: page by cursor
blocks.legend: The timeline carried ids only; the content, and with it deletion and visibility, comes from the post cache at render time.

blocks.text: A miss on the post cache reads the posts store and writes back. The timeline list carries ids only, so deletion and visibility are decided at render time by the feed service from the content, never from the list.

The bottleneck is fan-out write volume: 46,000 appends per second at peak, bursting far higher when a popular author posts. The timeline cache is partitioned by user id across memory nodes, and appends are batched per target node, so one post to 10,000 followers becomes a few dozen batched calls rather than 10,000 separate ones.
Fan-out lag, from the post event to the last append, is the freshness SLI. The 5 s target bounds the queue depth, and the workers scale on lag, not on CPU.

blocks.title: Why the celebrity exception exists
items: An account with 10 million followers posts.
Without the exception, that is 10 million appends from a single post.
At the whole fleet's peak capacity of 46,000 appends per second, that one post takes about 217 seconds, or 3.6 minutes, of everything.

The exception skips fan-out above 1 million followers (assumption): the post service compares the author's follower count with the threshold at post time, the post event carries the flag, the workers skip a flagged event, and the post is merged at read time, found by the author id in the list of celebrities the follower follows.

blocks.text: Reads are cheap by construction, one cached list plus one batched content fetch, so the read path scales by adding feed service replicas and cache replicas. The ranking call is the only expensive step; it is bounded by a deadline and degrades to chronological order.

Backfill for new followers is lazy: the follow call marks the followee pending, and the follower's next read merges the followee's last 48 hours of post ids into the timeline and clears the mark, not pushed at follow time, so a wave of follows after a viral moment does not become a write storm.
Each row names the failure, what the reader sees, and the mitigation.

the post id is appended to a timeline twice

blocks.text: At this scale a feed freshness SLO and the cost per daily active user become the numbers the team is held to, and the celebrity threshold becomes a tuning knob rather than a constant: lowering it moves cost from fan-out compute to read-time merging, and the right setting is the one that keeps the feed-open p99 inside its budget at the lowest total.

L1: Fan-out on write with a bounded timeline cache per user, and the celebrity exception stated with a threshold.
A post store separate from the timeline lists, with posts written once and referenced by id.
Cursor paging on time-ordered ids, and the fan-out arithmetic (400 million appends per day from the stated assumptions).
L2: Ranking as a separate service with a deadline and a chronological fallback.
Timeline cache sizing (128 GB) and the lazy backfill for new followers.
Fan-out lag as the freshness SLI and the scaling signal, with batched appends per cache node.
The tail-at-scale argument for why read-time assembly from 200 accounts misses the p99 target.
L3: The feed freshness SLO and a cost per daily active user as the constraints set before the design.
Cells for the timeline cache and the move toward read-time assembly as the follower graph grows.
What the cache must never decide: visibility and deletion are checked at render time, not at fan-out time.

interview_frame.title: A 45-minute interview
items: 0:00 to 0:05: Requirements: ask about ranking, freshness, the follower distribution, deletes and offline users. Say the numbers aloud: 230 posts per second at peak, 11,600 feed reads per second at peak, 46,000 timeline appends per second at peak, a 128 GB timeline cache.
0:05 to 0:10: Entities and API: Post, Follow (indexed both ways), Timeline; the four endpoints; cursor paging on time-ordered ids.

0:10 to 0:20: High-level design with the diagram: write path (post store, event, fan-out workers, timeline cache) and read path (feed service, celebrity merge, ranking, content cache). Name the hybrid fan-out as the central decision.

0:20 to 0:40: Two deep dives: fan-out volume and the celebrity threshold (batched appends, lag-based scaling, the 10-million-follower arithmetic), then the read path (one cached list, the ranking deadline and fallback, lazy backfill, render-time visibility checks).

0:40 to 0:45: Failure modes from the table, the 10x plan (cells, two-stage ranking, a lower celebrity threshold), and the L3 sentence: the timeline cache is a derived view; the SLO that matters is fan-out lag, and the cost that matters is per daily active user.
Context and scope: The product's follow graph, the current feed implementation if any, the ranking service's contract, and the freshness complaints or cost that motivate the design.
Goals and non-goals: Feed open p99 of 200 ms, visibility within 5 s, read availability of 99.9 percent; search, messaging, media and the ranking model are out of scope.
Design: This answer fills it: the hybrid fan-out, the timeline cache, the read path with ranking deadline, the data model and cursor paging.
Alternatives considered: Fan-out on read for everyone (FollowFeed shape), ranking at fan-out time, push-at-follow backfill, with the trade-off table.

Cross-cutting concerns: Observability (fan-out lag, cache hit ratio, unranked response rate), privacy (visibility checked at render), cost per daily active user, rollout by user cohort with the old feed as fallback.
Review questions the doc must answer: What happens when an account crosses the celebrity threshold mid-day, and how a deleted or restricted post is kept out of every reader's feed.
